# XLSX creation, editing, and analysis

| Task | Approach |
|---|---|
| **Create** or **edit** with formulas/formatting | `openpyxl` — see gotchas below |
| **Bulk data** in or out | `pandas` (`read_excel`, `to_excel`) |
| **Quick look** at a sheet | `markitdown file.xlsx` — `## SheetName` per sheet; reads `.xlsm` too. No cell coordinates, so don't plan edits from it |
| **Read** a model (formulas *and* values) | two `load_workbook` passes — see gotchas |

> `openpyxl`, `pandas`, and `markitdown` are preinstalled — do not run `pip install` first; write the script and import directly. Only if an import fails (or the `markitdown` command is missing): `pip install` the missing package.

> Script paths below are relative to this skill's directory.

## Requirements for every output

- **Professional font** (Arial, Times New Roman) throughout, unless the user says otherwise.
- **Zero formula errors.** Never ship while `recalc.py` reports `errors_found`. If you think an error predates you, prove it: load the *original* with `data_only=True` and look at that cell. An error you introduced looks exactly like one you inherited.
- **Use formulas, never hardcoded results.** Write `sheet['B10'] = '=SUM(B2:B9)'`, not the Python-computed total. The sheet must recalculate when its inputs change.
- **Follow the user's spec literally.** Exact tab names, exact column headers, and the formula they spelled out. A redesign that computes something else fails, however elegant.
- **Document every assumption and hardcoded number** where the reader will see it — a cell comment, or an adjacent cell at a table's end. Cite a real source when one exists (`Source: Company 10-K, FY2024, Page 45, Revenue Note, [SEC EDGAR URL]`); when the number came from the user, say so plainly.
- **A workbook *you create* for someone to fill in** needs a short legend naming which cells to edit, and one example row of realistic values showing the expected format. Never add such a row to a file you were asked to edit.
- **Editing an existing file: match its conventions exactly.** They override every guideline here. Find its designated input cells first — a distinct font color, fill, or shading marks them — write only there, and leave every existing formula untouched.

## Recalculate (mandatory whenever the file contains formulas)

openpyxl writes formulas as strings with **no cached values**. Until you recalculate, every
formula cell reads back as `None` to anything reading cached values — `pandas`,
`load_workbook(data_only=True)`, and most previewers.

```bash
python scripts/recalc.py output.xlsx [timeout_seconds]   # default 30
```

LibreOffice computes every formula, the file is **rewritten in place**, and you get JSON:
`status` (`success` | `errors_found`), `total_formulas`, `total_errors`, and an
`error_summary` naming up to 100 cells per error type (`locations_truncated` says how many it
withheld — trust `total_errors`, not the length of the list). Fix what it names and run it
again. **JSON with an `error` key instead of a `status` means nothing was recalculated**, and
only that case exits non-zero — `errors_found` exits 0, so never treat a clean exit as a clean
workbook.

**A green recalc proves your formulas *evaluate*, not that they are *right*.** An off-by-one
range or a reference to the wrong row yields a clean, error-free file with wrong numbers.
Write 2–3 formulas first and check they pull the values you expect, before building out a grid.

**A workbook that links to another file loses those links** if you re-save it with openpyxl and
then recalculate. Such a formula reads `='[1]Returns Analysis'!$B$2` — the `[1]` is an index
into the workbook's external-reference list, naming a *separate file on disk*, not a sheet.
That file is rarely present here, so the cell's cached value is the only thing holding its
data. openpyxl strips that value on save; LibreOffice then has to resolve the reference for
real, fails, writes `#NAME?`, and deletes every link. `recalc.py` refuses to run in that state
— copy those cells' values out of the original before you save over them (`--force` overrides,
and accepts the loss).

## Choosing formulas that survive verification

LibreOffice implements fewer functions than Excel, and one it cannot evaluate becomes a
literal `#NAME?` baked into the file you deliver.

- **Prefer Excel-2007-era functions** — `SUMIFS`, `INDEX`, `MATCH`, `IFERROR`, `SUMPRODUCT` — which need no prefix.
- **Six post-2007 functions work, but only with an `_xlfn.` prefix**, because openpyxl writes your formula into the XML verbatim and Excel stores post-2007 names prefixed (its UI hides the prefix): `_xlfn.TEXTJOIN`, `_xlfn.CONCAT`, `_xlfn.IFS`, `_xlfn.SWITCH`, `_xlfn.MAXIFS`, `_xlfn.MINIFS`. Written bare, each yields `#NAME?`.
- **Never use `XLOOKUP`, `XMATCH`, `SORT`, `FILTER`, `UNIQUE`, or `SEQUENCE`.** The runtime's LibreOffice cannot evaluate them under *any* prefix. Newer builds do evaluate them, but they are spilling array functions and an openpyxl-written file has no spill metadata, so only the top-left cell of the range gets a value — and `recalc.py` reports `total_errors: 0` on the truncated result. Use `INDEX`/`MATCH` for lookups, and sort, filter, and de-duplicate in Python before writing the cells.
- A formula LibreOffice could not parse is written back **lowercased** — a quick tell beside a `#NAME?`.

## openpyxl gotchas

- **Reading a model takes two loads.** `data_only=True` yields cached values with the formulas gone; the default yields formula strings with no values. One pass cannot give you both.
- **`data_only=True` is destructive if you save.** That workbook has no formulas left, so saving replaces every one with a literal — permanently.
- **`data_only=True` on a file openpyxl just wrote returns `None` everywhere** — run `recalc.py` first. (A formula whose result is `""` also reads back as `None`.)
- **Merged cells: write the top-left anchor only.** Every other cell in the range is a `MergedCell` whose `.value` is read-only.
- **`.xlsm` loses its macros unless you pass `keep_vba=True`** to `load_workbook`.
- **A sheet name containing a space must be quoted** in a cross-sheet reference: `='Assumptions Inputs'!$B$5`. Unquoted, it evaluates to `#VALUE!`.

## Financial models

Unless the user says otherwise, or the existing file already does something else.

**Color:** blue text (`0,0,255`) for hardcoded inputs and scenario levers · black for formulas ·
green (`0,128,0`) for links to another sheet · red (`255,0,0`) for links to another file ·
yellow fill (`255,255,0`) for key assumptions and cells the user should fill in.

**Numbers:** currency `$#,##0`, with the unit named in the header (`Revenue ($mm)`) · zeros
render as `-`, including in percentages (`$#,##0;($#,##0);-`) · negatives in parentheses ·
percentages `0.0%`, **stored as fractions** (`0.15` renders `15.0%`; storing `15` renders
`1500.0%`) · valuation multiples `0.0x` · years as text (`"2024"`, never `2,024`).

**Structure:** every assumption in its own labeled cell, referenced by the formulas that use it
(`=B5*(1+$B$6)`, never `=B5*1.05`) · formulas consistent across every projection period, since a
lone edited cell mid-row is the commonest silent error · guard denominators that can be zero.

`openpyxl`, `pandas`, `markitdown` (pip, preinstalled — install only if an import fails or the command is missing) · LibreOffice (`soffice`, auto-configured for sandboxed environments via `scripts/office/soffice.py`)

A permission denial, a dropped view or a statement timeout all produce `data = null` → `rows = []` → `return null`, and the entire "Inventory Forensic Audit" section **vanishes from the Command Center with no message at all**.
```js
const { data, error } = await supabase.from("document_search").select(...)...;
if (error) setErr(error.message); else setRows(data ?? []);
```

Three distinct states — loading, error (with the message on screen), and genuinely-empty — never collapsed into one. I will use this on every read on the new page, plus the section `&lt;Boundary&gt;` (App.jsx:482–504) which already reports crashes to `tg_log_client_error` rather than white-screening. **I will add no new `?? ## 5 · What I need from the view — and a finding that changes the brief

### ⛔ Read this before you build the view

**Computed from `metrc_plants` alone, this page prints "0 unexplained" for every room, and is structurally incapable of ever printing anything else.**

I measured all 16 room-cycles in the plant mirror, cohorted by `(raw-&gt;&gt;'LocationName', raw-&gt;&gt;'FloweringDate')`:

| | |
|---|---|
| Cohorts with `flipped = harvested + still standing` **exactly** | **16 of 16** |
| Destroyed plants inside any flower-room cohort | **1** (Flower Room #4, flipped 2025-12-03) |
| Unexplained under the naive arithmetic | **0 everywhere** |

That identity holds because `metrc_plants` is a **current-state mirror**: a plant destroyed mid-flower is removed from it, so it is subtracted from `flipped` and from `harvested` simultaneously. The arithmetic cannot fail. A check that cannot fail proves nothing.

The evidence that plants *are* going missing sits in two other places:

**(a) `metrc_rpt_plants_destroyed` — 3,773 rows, and the API mirror has never heard of them.**

| Location | Destroyed rows | Also present in `metrc_plants` |
|---|---|---|
| Vegetation Room | 2,371 | 0 |
| Mother Room | 560 | 97 |
| Flower Room #4 | 437 | **0** |
| Flower Room #2 | 255 | **0** |
| Flower Room #3 | 114 | **0** |
| Flower Room #1 | 35 | **0** |
| *(blank location)* | 1 | 0 |

**`destroyed_on` is NULL on all 3,773 rows.** The only usable date is `phase_date` (date the plant entered the phase it was destroyed from), and for flower rooms those land 2024-03-14 → 2025-12-03 — **exactly one** of which overlaps a mirror cohort. So today the destroyed register and the plant mirror cover almost disjoint eras, and the page must say so rather than net them to zero.

**(b) The harvest records carry their own plant count and disagree with the mirror.** `v_harvest_forensic.plants`, room-attributed the same way `v_room_turn_audit` does it (`harvest_name ilike '%'||grow_rooms.code`), window 2025-11-01 → 2026-08-11:

| Room | Plants on harvest records | Plants harvested in mirror | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| F1 | 3,610 | 4,068 | **+458** |
| F2 | 3,479 | 2,665 | **−814** |
| F3 | 4,185 | 2,763 | **−1,422** |
| F4 | 3,472 | 3,019 | **−453** |

Those windows are not cohort-aligned, so treat the magnitudes as indicative of a real disagreement, not as the answer. But the disagreement is the page.

**Also binding on the view:**
- **The cycle key must match `v_room_turn_audit`** — `grow_rooms.code` × `harvest_started`, with `f_rule('room_cycle_days')` for the 56-day rule. If this page invents its own cycle boundary, two Cultivation pages will disagree about what a pull is.

Please expose state from `raw-&gt;&gt;'State'`, and note that `v_room_plant_counts` and `HarvestLaborCalculator` may be reading the flat column.

## How I'd build the gate

Caps as owner-set rows, never code — material × licence × cap × restock level × basis. Three states:

- **Under restock** → allocation approved normally
- **Between restock and cap** → approved, flagged as filling
- **At or over cap** → **the approval is blocked, not warned.** A warning is something people click past. Your rule was "he gets no more" and that has to be a constraint.

The block lifts automatically when holdings fall to the restock level, so nobody has to remember to re-open it. Every block writes a row saying what was requested, what the cap was, and what they were holding — so if it's wrong you can see it, and if they're being starved unfairly the evidence is there too.

## Why tags disappear

`metrc-sync` v19, verbatim from its own notes:

> *"KNOWN LIMITATION, stated honestly rather than papered over: **a partial sweep does NOT resume. Each run re-walks from page 1.** 'Run again to continue' makes progress only because later runs get further before the deadline."*

The mechanics:

| | |
|---|---|
| Page size | **20 rows** |
| Pause between pages | 200 ms |
| Soft deadline | **110 seconds** |
| `plants` paths, in order | vegetative → flowering → **onhold** → **inactive** |

**`inactive` runs last of four.** Every run re-walks vegetative, flowering and onhold from page one, *then* starts inactive — and dies in roughly the same place every time. At 20 rows a page with a 200 ms pause, it never gets deep into the inactive list.

**That is your bimodal signature explained exactly.** Metrc returns inactive plants in a fixed order; the sweep always captures the front of that list and never the back. Whole harvests land or don't, depending on which side of the cut they fall. Strawberry Biscotti is past the cut. Chimera isn't.

Nothing is lost in Metrc. **We have been fetching the same first pages over and over for months.**

## And the fix needs no new code

The function **already accepts `winStart` and `winEnd`**. Windowed runs are supported today:

```
metrc-sync?endpoints=plants&winStart=2025-11-01T00:00:00Z&winEnd=2025-12-01T00:00:00Z
```

Narrow the window to a month and vegetative/flowering/onhold return almost nothing, so the full 110 seconds goes to `inactive` — and a month of inactive plants fits comfortably. **Walk the history one month at a time and the 6,023 come back.**

That's a backfill I can run against the existing, proven function. No deploy, no schema change, no rolled-back v18 resume cursor.

## Same code confirms the clone bug

The `plantbatches` mapper reads:

```
count: r.UntrackedCount ?? r.Count
```

`UntrackedCount` is **zero on an emptied batch**, which is why all 691 historical clone batches read as zero clones. **`TrackedCount` is never mapped at all.** Exactly what I measured this morning, now with the line of code that causes it.

I'd expect the gap to close to near zero. If it doesn't — if a window comes back complete and plants are *still* missing — then we have a real question, and we'll have earned the right to ask it.

**Say go and I'll start with December 2025 and report the before-and-after count.**

## Why we don't have them

Metrc serves packages in four buckets: **active · on hold · inactive · in transit.** A package that shipped and was received by a customer moves to **inactive** at your licence. It still exists in Metrc forever — that's seed to sale, and you're right that Metrc knows every one of them.

Our mirror holds:

| Bucket | Packages |
|---|---:|
| inactive | 3,431 |
| active | 551 |
| in transit | 402 |
| **total** | **4,384** |

The sync walks those four paths **in order, 20 rows per page, 200 ms between pages, against a 110-second deadline that only checks between pages.** `inactive` is third of four and by far the largest — it's every package you've ever shipped. It never reaches the end. Then the next run starts from page 1 again, because the function's own header says *"a partial sweep does NOT resume."*

**We have been re-fetching the first few thousand inactive packages over and over and never seeing the rest.** Identical to the plants, and now proven twice.

```
\{(?:[^{}]|\{[^{}]*\})*\}
```

But the handler is three deep:

```js
onKeyDown={(e) => { if (e.key === "Enter") { e.preventDefault(); setDrill(r); } }}
//        1        2                        3
```

So the attribute doesn't match, the scanner falls through to `[^<>'"]`, and **terminates the tag at the `>` inside `=>`** — never seeing `onKeyDown`. Both flagged elements have a three-level key handler. Fixing the scanner, with a fixture.

## 2. Key Technical Concepts

- **Supabase/Postgres**: 371 tables, 415 views, 18 matviews, 723 policies; RLS enabled on every public table; `db_policy` (11 hard rules); `db_change_review` requiring 3 non-proposer approvals; `v_db_change_status`.
- **Metrc API v2**: `/plants/v2/{vegetative,flowering,onhold,inactive}`, `/packages/v2/{active,onhold,inactive,intransit}`, `/plantbatches/v2/{active,inactive}`; `lastModifiedStart`/`lastModifiedEnd` windowing; PAGE_SIZE 20; 110s soft deadline.
- **Edge functions** (27 live): `metrc-sync` v19, `parse-documents` v7, `coa-inspect`, `apex-sync`, `apex-probe`.
- **40-gate CI chain** in `netlify.toml` (`npm run gates` → `tools/checks/run-gates.mjs`), fail-fast; six gates DEGRADE without a database.
- **Ratchets not cliffs**: baselines may fall, never rise.
- **Fixtures**: both halves required (positive fires, negative stays quiet); `trg_require_fixture` on `checker_registry`.
- **Backfill pattern**: `backfill_watch` (`remaining_sql`, `accepted_floor`, `floor_reason`) + `backfill_reading`.
- **Owner rulings**: D4 (identity is the tag), 4A (name the licensee, never "ours"), C0 (ownership stops at the COA), C6d (tolled material never counts as ours), J6 (two independent checkpoints), K1 (the five questions).

```ts
let OURS: string[] = [];
async function loadOurLicences(sb: ReturnType<typeof createClient>): Promise<void> {
  const { data, error } = await sb.from("company_licenses").select("license").eq("active", true);
  if (error) throw new Error("company_licenses unreadable: " + error.message);
  const found = (data ?? []).map((r: { license: string }) => r.license).filter(Boolean);
  if (!found.length) {
    throw new Error("company_licenses returned no active licences. Refusing to parse - every origin would be misclassified as a destination and every manifest would name us as the counterparty.");
  }
  OURS = found;
}
```

**Modified — `tools/checks/accessibility.mjs`** — replaced the regex tag scanner with a balanced scan:
```js
function openingTags(src) {
  const tags = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < src.length; i++) {
    if (src[i] !== "<") continue;
    const nm = /^<([A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9.]*)/.exec(src.slice(i, i + 64));
    if (!nm) continue;
    let j = i + nm[0].length, depth = 0, quote = null, end = -1;
    for (; j < src.length; j++) {
      const c = src[j];
      if (quote) { if (c === quote && src[j - 1] !== "\\") quote = null; continue; }
      if (c === "'" || c === '"' || c === "`") { quote = c; continue; }
      if (c === "{") { depth++; continue; }
      if (c === "}") { depth--; continue; }
      if (c === ">" && depth === 0) { end = j; break; }
      if (c === "<" && depth === 0) break;
    }
    if (end < 0) continue;
    let attrs = src.slice(i + nm[0].length, end);
    if (attrs.endsWith("/")) attrs = attrs.slice(0, -1);
    tags.push({ name: nm[1], attrs, index: i });
    i = end;
  }
  return tags;
}
```

## 4. Errors and Fixes

1. **Anon surface 656 relations** — was a privilege-row count, not relations. Re-derived two ways: 6 views, all `security_invoker`. Caught before reporting.
2. **Domain coverage 356 unowned** — I ran LIKE patterns as regex, so `metrc_%` could never match. Corrected to 243.
3. **"Tile says 40 vs live 48"** — `open_questions` holds 40 `open` + 8 `answered`; the tile was right. Withdrawn on the record; logged in `check_defect`.
4. **"$199,000/year from F2/F4 running 100 short"** — 1,150 is the facility-wide "Operating Est.", not per-room capacity. Withdrawn.
5. **"The OS cannot see the clone stage"** — `metrc_plant_batches` exists with 754 rows; `sync_item.target` says `metrc_plantbatches` (no underscore), which is why I missed it.
6. **"9 of 16 room-cycles below floor"** — measured our data loss, not room shortfall. Withdrawn.
7. **795-plant gap** — INNER join hid 54 harvests with zero. Real: 6,023 windowed / 36,725 all-time. I had written the FULL OUTER JOIN rule into Agent S's brief that morning.
8. **CRITICAL "supplier names wrong both directions"** — `v_stock_on_hand.supplier` is `received_from` = "delivered by", not "made by". Trap 1 in a document written four hours earlier. Withdrawn, `check_defect` logged as `wrong_population`/`false_alarm`.
9. **"ALL 40 GATES PASSED" locally** — vacuous: `merge-base HEAD origin/main` = HEAD, so theme-lock compared the file to itself. Re-verified with `TG_THEME_BASE` pinned and `.mcp.json` moved aside.
10. **Nearly re-shipped a data-destruction bug** — drift gate said "deploy parse-documents"; repo was v4/v5-era, production v6 with the regression fix. Read production first, merged, deployed v7.
11. **Two baselines committed** — one staged as a rename then deleted from disk; `git ls-files` showed both.
12. **My own driver bug** — in-flight check hardcoded `'plants%'`; fixed before packages windows were queued.

## What materiality actually is

It's the line where an error stops being a nuisance and starts being a lie. Formally: **the size at which a misstatement would change what someone does** — you, a lender, the IRS, the Commission.

Every audit firm sets it. The reason isn't laziness, it's the opposite: without a declared line, "we checked everything" is a bluff, and every argument becomes about whether a given error mattered — argued *after* you know the answer, which is how numbers get talked away.

## The three numbers and what each one does

**$71,000 — planning materiality.** The scoping number. Set before any testing. It answers *how hard do we look*: an account that can't be wrong by $71,000 gets a light touch; one that can gets the full procedure. It's 1% of $7,146,829 — revenue is the right benchmark for you because 280E distorts pre-tax income so badly it's useless as a base.

**$25,000 — inventory and COGS materiality.** Deliberately tighter, and this is the whole 280E point. In a normal manufacturer, an inventory error moves taxable income only through the margin — overstate inventory by $100k and maybe $30k of income moves. **Under 280E almost nothing is deductible except COGS, so an inventory error flows to taxable income close to dollar-for-dollar.** The same mistake costs you roughly three times what it costs a normal company. So the threshold has to be about a third.

**$3,500 — clearly trivial.** Below this, an individual difference gets written in the working papers and not chased. **But it still gets accumulated** — and that's the part people miss. A thousand $200 errors is $200,000. You compare the *running total* of everything you left alone against the $71,000, not each item.

## The one rule that makes it work

**Set before testing. Never after.** A threshold chosen once you've seen the finding isn't materiality, it's a finding being made to disappear. Your $1.00 manifest rounding tolerance is the correct precedent — declared in advance, applied blind.

## Where it does *not* apply at all

No dollar threshold on an untagged plant, an unmanifested transfer, an undocumented destruction, or anything touching a licence number. **One is a finding.** A regulator doesn't net a diversion against turnover. That's already in the database as definitional, not provisional.

| Third-party material with no usable cost | 1,820 lb | Inventory | Blocks the COGS number |
| Nova Farms $0.01 placeholder | $0.01 | Below trivial | Note it, don't chase it |
| 79.3 lb unexplained | weight | **No threshold applies** | Completeness — explain regardless |

## The problem you should know about

**The base is in dispute.** I set $71,000 as 1% of $7,146,829 — but your two revenue derivations differ by $97,256, and *that difference is itself larger than the materiality it would set*. Circular. It doesn't invalidate the number as a working figure, but a real auditor would resolve revenue first and then set the line.

## The assertion framework — what merging it actually means

An **assertion** is a claim your numbers make. Every audit procedure exists to test one. There are only seven or eight, and they're the complete set — which is what makes them useful, because you can *prove coverage*.

"Is the inventory right?" can't be answered. Broken into assertions it can:

- **Existence** — the 847 lb we say we hold is physically there
- **Completeness** — everything we hold is *on* the list *(the hard one — you can't find missing rows by looking at present ones)*
- **Accuracy** — grams read as grams, not pounds
- **Rights** — it's ours, not tolled or 3PL
- **Cutoff** — it landed in the right year
- **Presentation** — the tile doesn't mislead
- **Authorisation** — someone entitled to approve it did

**Why merge:** right now the same framework exists twice — D's A1–A7 in a markdown file, mine as `audit_assertion` in the database with controls, a coverage view and passing fixtures. Two copies drift, and this place has been burned by exactly that (two fleets, two baselines, two revenue figures). **The split I recommend:** D's codes and incident anchors are better written than mine. My table is the only version that can *enforce*. So D's content goes into my table, the markdown becomes doctrine-only, and one thing is authoritative.

**Why Authorisation must be A8:** D's seven have no assertion for *"who approved this."* Your allotment rule — only Admin, CEO or CFO — is an authorisation control. So is the 3-reviewer schema gate. ## How the three companies solve it — and what I built

They converge on one answer, a **semantic layer**:

- **QuickBooks** — one ledger. Every report is a *projection* of the journal, never a recomputation. Two definitions of revenue cannot exist because a report is not permitted to invent a number.
- **Microsoft** — one semantic model; DAX measures defined once, referenced by name, with a *Certified* endorsement and queryable lineage.
- **Google/Looker** — LookML. `measure: pounds_on_hand` is declared once. A dashboard **cannot** re-implement it — re-implementation is not expressible in the language. That's the strongest property of the three.

So: `metric_definition` — one canonical definition per figure, with its **population rule in words** (most disagreements aren't arithmetic, they're two populations answering two questions), its owner, and a certification that requires a signature and a date.

## AGENT I

My honest view: **you're right, and your own reference screenshots prove it.** The designs you loved — the rings, the dense KPI grid header, the monospace footer — are all *tight*. Big type with lots of air reads as a consumer app; density reads as an instrument. Bloomberg, trading desks, air-traffic screens — serious operational tools are dense because operators want maximum signal per glance. A cannabis ops platform run like a police state should look like one.

But there's a right and a wrong way to shrink:

**Wrong:** zoom everything down 20% per page. You get inconsistency (the disease we just measured in the date selectors), broken layouts, and text nobody over 40 can read on the facility floor.

**Right — a density system, one change, site-wide:**

1. **Shrink through the spacing and type tokens, in one place** — paddings, gaps, and the type scale drop together, every page inherits, consistency is structural. No per-page hacks, ever.
2. **Keep the hierarchy ratio.** The professional look isn't small numbers — it's *contrast*: KPI figures stay commanding while labels, context lines and chrome get small and quiet. Shrink the quiet parts hardest.
3. **A floor:** nothing below ~12px, contrast preserved — the accessibility gate we just fixed stays green. Cramped-but-legible is professional; squinting is not.
4. **Two density modes, per user** like your collapse state: **Compact** (default for management — your Big Daddy view) and **Comfortable** (floor staff on tablets, where touch targets matter). Costs almost nothing extra once it's tokens.

One procedural note: sizes live in the guarded theme files, and the theme-lock gate will trip on any change — correctly, that's its job. With your order, the baseline gets updated *deliberately*, once, on the record — colours and fonts stay frozen; only scale and spacing move.

**Recommendation: do it, as tokens, Compact by default.** Say go and B gets the spec folded into the current build so everything ships dense the first time rather than being shrunk after.

```sql
-- The view's chosen row for the 7 offenders is always the MC281714 side:
with pk as (

         coalesce(p.finished,false) fin, p.quantity, p.raw-&gt;&gt;'LastModified' lm
  from metrc_packages p
```

## What that means, plainly

**COGS cannot be computed today.** Direct labour needs hours (zero). Materials need purchases (zero). Under 280E, COGS is your *only* surviving deduction — so this is the largest money exposure in the company, and it's data entry, not engineering.

**Margins follow COGS** — they can't exist before it. **Staff can't be micromanaged** — a roster is a list of names, not an operating picture, without schedules and hours.

## The order I'd work it

1. **Packaging supply — the cheapest win.** 15 items already modelled with reorder levels. It needs consumption rules so stock falls as product is packed; then low-stock alerting works immediately. Days, not weeks.
2. **Time capture.** The highest-value feed in the company: one input unlocks labour hours, payroll cost, 280E labour substantiation, *and* real scheduling.
3. **Purchase capture** — your IRC 6001 evidence gap.

## The approval gate — agents can no longer change data

`correction_proposal`. Every flagged issue must answer **six questions**, enforced by the database:

1. **The issue** — with the measurement
2. **The evidence** — re-runnable SQL and the numbers, so you can check it yourself
3. **What needs fixing** — the exact object and rows
4. **The proposal** — precisely what would be done
5. **Why this is the fix** — *the mechanism.* Which cause it removes, and how they know that's the real cause and not a symptom that correlates
6. **How it never repeats** — a **named** guard: a check, a trigger, a constraint, a registry row. *"Be careful next time" is rejected.*

And the gate has teeth: **a proposal cannot reach "applied" without passing through "approved"** — refused by trigger, not convention. Only you can approve. A rejection requires a reason so the next agent doesn't propose it again. An applied change must name the migration that carried it.

## What was already there

`widget_catalog` holds **45 widgets**, and they're well made — **every single one has a drill target, zero exceptions.** Each carries its source table, aggregation, format and drill route:

| Category | Widgets | Examples |
|---|---:|---|

**Nobody has ever saved a layout.** The table is empty. The catalogue and the save path were built and the front end was never wired to either.

## Why your trading-platform comparison changed the answer

The old storage held `position` and `span` — a one-dimensional flow. It can reorder tiles and set a width. It **cannot** place a panel in two dimensions, which is the whole point of a terminal layout. It also had **no user column**, so two executives could never hold different views — which your own rule 5 already requires.

So I built the real thing: a **12-column grid with x, y, w, h per widget, per page, per user.** Move and resize freely, saved to your login. Row-level security binds every row to its owner, so nobody can read or alter anyone else's arrangement. The grid enforces `x + w ≤ 12`, so a saved layout can never overflow its own canvas.

Two functions alongside it: save a page atomically — a layout is one arrangement, and a half-saved one leaves you looking at a screen you never chose — and **reset to the house default**, because anyone who drags a panel somewhere useless needs a way back.

A widget disabled in the catalogue vanishes from every saved layout at once. That's how a retired tile actually retires, instead of lingering on three people's dashboards.

## My recommendation on sequencing

**Let B finish restoring the Command Center drills first, then build the grid.** You set the rule that Command Center has to be 100% before anything else moves, and the drag-and-resize canvas is a substantial front-end piece — react-grid-style layout, drag handles, resize corners, persistence on drop. Dropping it on B mid-repair is how the tiles went inert in the first place.

The data layer is done and waiting, so the moment the drills are green this is a front-end job with nothing to design.

### 1. Agent P's diagnosis is half right, and the wrong half is the expensive one

**Verified:** 12 runs failed with that exact message. **Not verified — it is wrong:** they were not spread over six days. All 12 fell inside **thirteen minutes on 5 Aug (17:16–17:29)**. The original error is fully explained: the table was created 4 Aug with `unique (license, package_tag, test_type, result_date)`; migration `20260805165312` added nullable `test_name` with no index; `metrc-lab-sync` upserts `onConflict: license,package_tag,test_name`. Postgres refused a key that did not exist.

Then someone created `metrc_lab_results_license_pkg_testname_key` — a unique index on exactly those three columns, **ad hoc, outside any migration file** (it appears only in the 12 Aug baseline dump). The error stopped.

**That index is the real damage.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Result rows Metrc returned (`metrc_lab_backfill.results`, error-free fetches) | **119,167** |
| Result rows we actually hold (`metrc_lab_results`) | **101,608** |
| **Fetched from the legal record and silently discarded** | **17,559 (14.7%)** |

137 packages lost every row; 3 lost part (894 rows). Mechanism: a package inherits results from its whole lineage, so it carries many certificates; per certificate Metrc returns ~40 analytes and `TestTypeName` repeats across certificates of the same product category. `metrc-lab-backfill` writes with `.insert()`, so one repeated name rejects the whole 200-row batch and the error is swallowed (`if (error &amp;&amp; errs.length &lt; 3) errs.push(...)` — then `fetched_at` is stamped anyway).

The correlation is decisive:

| certificates on the package | landed | lost |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1,885 | 5 |
| 2 | 16 | 30 |
| 3 or more | 3 | 21 |

And **every one of the 2,642 tags that landed has exactly as many rows as it has distinct test names** (2,642 of 2,642). That is not a property of lab testing; it is the shape of the index.

So the constraint was not missing — it was **wrong**, and adding it converted a loud failure into a silent one. Same rule as always (never pick a key to make an error stop), running in the unfamiliar direction.

`metrc_backfill_window` is a **`lastModified` date-window** queue and `tg_metrc_backfill_next()` fires `metrc-sync?endpoints=&lt;endpoint&gt;&amp;winStart=…`. The per-package queue for this already exists: `metrc_lab_backfill`. It needs an enqueuer, a re-enqueuer, and a cron — which is what the migration adds.

# Blocker 1 — dump-schema.mjs, root cause and fix

**Not credentials, not `statement_timeout`, not a pooler idle-drop.** The keepalive you added was reasonable and could not have worked, because the connection was never idle.

The killer was the **VIEWS section's recursive CTE**. It walked the view dependency graph with `UNION ALL` and no de-duplication, so it enumerated every distinct **path** rather than every node — and `pg_depend` stores one row per referenced *column*, so our 278 real edges present as 2,037. Measured, live:

| depth | rows | | depth | rows |
|---|---:|---|---|---:|
| 0 | 484 | | 3 | 55,357 |
| 1 | 2,037 | | 4 | 112,766 |
| 2 | 12,125 | | 5 | 276,503 |

Against a cap of `depth &lt; 12` that is order 10⁹ rows in the recursive working table. The backend exhausts memory and is killed, so the client sees a dead socket **with no server error message** — which is the signature that told me it was a killed backend and not a timeout. At 225 views it was survivable. The query never changed; the schema grew into it.

**The fix captures more, not less:** de-duplicate the edge set, `UNION` instead of `UNION ALL`, and constrain the *consumer* side to the public schema (the old recursion did not, so a non-public view could be pulled in and emitted as `public.&lt;name&gt;` — a latent bug). Output is byte-identical: `max(depth) group by` never cared about duplicate paths.

**The walk went from ~10⁹ rows to 893.** Three consecutive clean runs, VIEWS at 5.3s / 4.3s / 2.6s.

Two silent failures fixed alongside it, both in my lane:

- The `pg` Client emits `error` as an **EventEmitter event**. With no listener Node terminated the process *before* the diagnostic `catch` could run — for exactly the failure it was written to explain. That is why you only ever saw one bare line.
- Every catalogue read is now named and timed, so a future failure prints which step died, how long it had run, and every step that completed. And the view count is **asserted against `pg_class` before the file is written** — a thin baseline is worse than a missing one, because a thin one looks like success.

You had ~36 hours of headroom you could not see: `MAX_AGE_HOURS = 48` in `schema-baseline-fresh.mjs`, and the last baseline was 12 Aug 12:03. From 14 Aug 12:03 that gate goes **hard red in Netlify** regardless of connection. With the dump broken it could not have been regenerated.

# The check that was wrong — and what I did about it

`check:docsdb` failed the build on **five real licences** in `docs/AUDIT_2024_INVENTORY_BALANCE.md`. All five are genuine Massachusetts counterparties, each attested by our own Metrc transfer records: two Flower Power Growers licences (54 and 11 transfers), Bud's Goods &amp; Service (150), Northeast Alternatives (1), Coastal Cultivars (5).

The check validated every MC/MP code against `company_licenses` — which holds *our* licences by definition and structurally cannot hold a customer's. An audit document listing who we shipped to could not be written without failing the build. Classic `wrong_population` / `false_alarm`, filed in `check_defect`.

**I widened the authority, not the tolerance.** The question is "does this licence exist?", and it was being put to a source that cannot hold half the right answers. Now: `company_licenses` **plus** counterparties Metrc can attest from real transfer rows. The verdict does not move — a code in neither set is still a hard fail, so the founding defect (a Metrc **user ID** typed with an MC prefix and mailed to `api-info@metrc.com`) is still caught.

Both halves of the fixture ship with it: 3 positive cases that must fail, 4 negative that must stay quiet. And I did the thing that actually proves it — **injected a fabricated licence into the live document, watched the gate fail with exit 1, then reverted.** Twice, once after refactoring the fixture. `git status` on `docs/` is clean.

No exemption granted, no baseline raised.

## The RPC and its gate

Three verbs, one definition each, all `SECURITY DEFINER` with `search_path` pinned:

- **`tg_set_secret(p_key text, p_value text)`** — store or replace. Signature unchanged so nothing breaks. Returns `void` deliberately: the page re-reads the registry and shows its state, so the screen cannot say "saved" about something that did not save.
- **`tg_secret_register(p_key, p_label, p_help)`** — name a key in plain English, no value.
- **`tg_secret_forget(p_key, p_drop_registration default false)`** — the rotate/delete path.

**Gate: `app_users.role in ('owner','executive')`, checked inside each function.**

## Proof the value cannot be read back

The view stops referencing the column — **absent, not masked**. The last-4 is computed once at write time into `app_secrets.value_last4`, and only when the value is ≥12 characters (below that, four characters is too much of the secret, so nothing is shown).

That makes it a property a check can assert, and a `DO` block asserts all three before the transaction may commit:

```sql
if pg_get_viewdef('public.v_secret_status'::regclass, true) ~ '\mvalue\M' then raise exception ...
if has_column_privilege('authenticated','public.app_secrets','value','SELECT') then raise exception ...
if has_function_privilege('authenticated','public.tg_read_secret(text)','EXECUTE') then raise exception ...
```

**I broke the guard and watched it catch** (rule 1), four shapes, run live:

| The current 11-char `left(value,7)` mask | **true** |
| A `right(value,4)` masked-in-SQL version | **true** |
| Qualified `s.value` | **true** |

## What I found before building, which saved most of the work

**Half of it already existed.** `spaces` has **8 real rows**, each with its own status set, colour and privacy. `tasks` was already ClickUp-shaped — space, watchers, recurrence, ordering, budget, tags, start and due dates. `task_dependencies`, `teams`, `channels` all there. Nobody had wired any of it.

So I built only the gap: **lists, comments with mentions, subtasks, checklists, attachments, time tracking, activity history, and saved views** (list / board / calendar / table / timeline, per user).

Three decisions worth naming:

**Subtasks are tasks with a parent**, in the same table. A subtask you can assign, date, comment on and time-track is what people actually want; a separate subtask table always disappoints.

**Logged minutes are a generated column**, computed from start and end. Logged time and the clock can never disagree, because nobody types the number.

**Workspace time is not payroll time.** Task time lives here; payroll lives in `time_entries` with the parked HR module. I've written into the schema that the two must never be summed — that's exactly the kind of thing that quietly becomes a wrong number six months from now.

## What I changed about the record

Your original report was wrong. Agent V's correction of the *mechanism* is right and I confirmed it independently. But Agent V's **severity** claim is partly wrong too, and there is a bigger defect underneath both.

**The mechanism (confirmed).** `nav_role_visibility` is a deny-list. 119 of 665 enabled pages carry no deny row. Not scattered — 82% of the gap is two modules, `hr` (73 of 87) and `reports` (25 of 35), built after the last sweep.

**The payroll exposure (partly refuted).** Agent V listed 18 sensitive pages as reachable by `qb_time_only`. At the data layer most are protected: Pay Runs, Pay Run Detail and Payroll Imports require `f_can_read_hr()`; Payroll Journal and Year to Date are `security_invoker=true` views so base RLS applies; Tax Profiles is self-or-HR; the Sensitive Access Log requires `f_caller_is_admin()`. **The menu was open; the data was not.** Only three genuinely leak: `deduction_codes` and `earning_codes` (policy is literally `using (true)`) and the CFO Dashboard.

## Three things worth more than the nav gap

**1. The worst item is a wrong label, and it is ours.** `v_page_wiring` computes `roles_who_can_see` by counting rows where `visible = true` — against an application that reads `visible = false`. So `v_report_standard` stamps **"FAILS - nobody can open it"** on 114 pages. All 114 are a subset of the 119 that are visible to *everyone*. Inverted, zero exceptions. And `ratchet_baseline.report_nobody_can_open = 114`, set by agent-w on 11 Aug, enshrines it. This is worse than a missing check: anyone acting on that label would add `visible=true` rows, which under a deny model change nothing — the fix would look successful and the exposure would persist.

**2. `ratchet_baseline.views_bypassing_rls` is in breach.** Baseline 215 set 11 Aug; the count today is **224**, all readable by `authenticated`. It rose by 9 and nothing alarmed. Per the `self_inflicted_ratchet` rule the answer is to find and flip those 9 — the ceiling does not move. This is the layer that actually enforces; the nav is a menu, and a user can call PostgREST directly and never load `App.jsx`.

**3. A code bypass nobody had named.** `App.jsx:11236` resolves `special[view]` *before* the `routable` filter, so 59 hardcoded routes ignore both the deny-list and `admin_only`. Four are `admin_only=true` and URL-reachable this way: `pay_runs`, `terminals`, `onboard`, `hr_review_queue`. Their base tables hold, so it is an open door into a locked room — still an open door. Agent B's lane.

## Your three questions

**Blast radius.** Not 32 employees at 7am. **A naive flip locks out the owner** — measured: owner 665 → 549 pages, cfo 652 → 320, employee 625 → 304. That is incomplete seeding, not a wrong model, and it would read as a platform outage rather than a permissions change.

**Exploited?** No, and not currently exploitable. `auth.users` holds **2 accounts, both `owner`**, last sign-in 6 Aug. Zero accounts hold `qb_time_only`. It arms itself when the first employee account is created. Separately: `sensitive_access_log` has **never held a row** — I could only rule out exploitation because the user list is two people; at 34 that argument is gone.

**The timing is the argument.** This work is free today and expensive the day after onboarding. That reason expires.

## Recommendation

**Classify to author, allow-list to enforce** — 120 decisions instead of 4,457, and the class *materialises* explicit rows rather than becoming a fourth runtime mechanism. Surviving: `role_capability`/`f_role_can` as the single definition of authority (already default-deny, already what RLS consumes), and `nav_role_visibility` demoted to menu reach. Retiring: `page_permissions` and `nav_registry.admin_only` — but **not before** the `special` bypass closes, because `page_permissions` is currently the only gate that applies to those 59 routes.

Three checks are specified with both fixture halves. On Check 2 the negative half has to be a constructed fixture because the safe case does not exist in live data — and that absence is precisely why nobody noticed the label was backwards.

One caveat I could not settle read-only: `current_app_role()` returns `readonly` for any authenticated user with no `app_users` row, and `readonly` reaches **610 of 665** pages. If self-signup is enabled on this project, that is the real default posture and it should be checked before onboarding.</result>

## Lights out on F2

One action shifts that pull **and every later pull in F2** by however many days, with your reason recorded on each. Those downstream pulls are then measured against the **new** dates — they don't spend the rest of the year reading LATE against a plan that stopped being achievable in week one.

## But slipping is still a violation

Two different things were being called one thing:

- **Disruption** — lights out, dead dryer, room lost. Plan was impossible. **Baseline moves.**
- **Slipping** — plan was fine, we missed it. **Original stands. Still a violation.**

Both keep the original date, always. So the record holds both facts at once: the plan was the 3rd, a disruption moved it to the 10th, we hit the 10th.

**So a room-day is worth 180 ÷ 56 = 3.21 lb.** That's the conversion everything hangs on.

## Question 1 — does early cancel late?

- **No offset:** 43 days × 3.21 = **138 lb**
- **Net of early:** 25 days × 3.21 = **80 lb**

My view: **don't offset.** Coming down 3 days early doesn't bank 3 days of room time — the next cycle doesn't start early, it starts when it's planted. Early protects quality; it doesn't create capacity. But you know the floor.

## Question 2 — and this is the big one — is $1,100 the right multiplier?

**$1,100 is what a pound *costs you to make*, not what it's worth.** If you don't produce a pound, you don't spend that $1,100 either.

What a lost pound actually costs is what you'd have **sold** it for, minus what you'd have **spent** making it. So I need your **selling price per pound** — and there isn't one in the platform anywhere I can find.

At a wholesale price of, say, $1,400, the loss is £300/lb of margin, not $1,100. **138 lb at $1,100 reads $152,000; at a $300 margin it's $41,400.** Same days, four times the difference.

Which number do you want on the Finance dashboard — lost revenue, lost margin, or cost of goods not made?

## Question 3 — do late days actually lose production, or absorb?

Four rooms on 56-day cycles is about **26 possible pulls a year**. You're scheduling **24**. That's roughly two pulls of slack.

So some lateness may absorb into the gaps rather than pushing a cycle out of the year. The honest version distinguishes **days late** (always true) from **cycles actually lost** (only when lateness exceeds the slack).

**My recommendation: report both.** "43 days late, which is 138 lb of room-time at risk, of which X translated into a cycle we didn't get." One is the discipline measure; the other is the money.

# Agent V — Verification report: schedule adherence KPIs

## Headline: I did not build the tiles, and I am recommending you do not either yet

Two reasons, in order of weight:

**1. The figures the build was to be founded on do not survive independent derivation.** `v_schedule_compliance` matches a scheduled pull to a harvest using a bare date window with **no room predicate**. On a four-room rotation taking a room down every ~13 days, that window almost always contains *another room's* takedown first — and because it takes `min()`, it is biased toward the earliest date, which **systematically understates lateness**. Building the owner's most-watched dashboard on it would publish wrong numbers in the lenient direction.

**2. Role.** My charter is read-only except `verification_checks`; I build nothing, because the agent who repairs is the agent who stops seeing. If I had built these tiles I could not then have been one of your three reviewers on them. I have instead done the part that is unambiguously mine and filed the blocker.

## The defect

`v_schedule_compliance.actual_date` is:

```sql
select min(h.harvest_start) from metrc_harvests h
 where coalesce(h.raw-&gt;&gt;'DryingLocationName','') &lt;&gt; ''
   and h.harvest_start &gt;= p.harvest_date - 5
   and h.harvest_start &lt;= p.harvest_date + 21
```

No room. No cultivar. A date window and `min()`.

**It matched the wrong room on 12 of the 15 pulls it resolved.** The last correct measurement it produced was pull 3, scheduled **8 February 2026**. Everything since is another room's harvest.

Three independent signals agree it is wrong: room parsed from the documented `TG &lt;strain&gt; - &lt;YYYYMMDD&gt; &lt;room&gt;` convention; cultivar overlap (room-aware match scores 3–6 cultivars in common, the view's match scores 0 or 1 on every disputed pull); and physical coherence (room-aware lateness rises monotonically 0→26 days, the signature of compounding).

Worked examples:

| pull | room | planned | view says | truth | evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | F1 | 05 Apr | **1 day late** (matched 06 Apr **F4**) | **22 days late** (F1 down 27 Apr) | 5 of 6 cultivars match |
| 11 | F1 | 31 May | **5 days EARLY** (matched 26 May **F3**) | **26 days late** (F1 down 26 Jun) | 4 of 5 cultivars match |
| 13 | F3 | 29 Jun | **3 days EARLY** (matched 26 Jun **F1**) | **25 days late** (F3 down 24 Jul) | 5 of 6, incl. the schedule's own "Moraccan Paches/Dirty Taxi" |
| 14 | F4 | 13 Jul | **3 days EARLY** (matched 10 Jul **F2**) | **31 days overdue, no harvest at all** | F4 not down since 08 Jun |

**Five pulls are currently published as EARLY.** Under the owner's asymmetric ruling early is acceptable and needs no explanation — so the view is actively waving through its worst violations. That is the most damaging possible direction for this specific error.

The `+21` ceiling also caps measurable lateness at 21 days, so pull 14's 31-day overdue **cannot be represented at all**.

## What I hit, and it is not new

Run 3150 (`plants (full sweep)`) is **still open at 398s against a 110s deadline**, records 0. Writes to `metrc_plants` stopped at 21:57:34 and nothing has landed since — so the function died and neither the soft deadline nor the `beforeunload` backstop closed the row. The stuck-run reaper will close it at 30 minutes.

This is **not a v20 regression**. Under v19, runs 3042, 3048 and 3058 show the identical signature — long-window plant runs, ~30 minutes open, records 0, closed by the reaper. v20 kept both defences unchanged and did not claim to fix this.

I think I have located it, though I have not proven it: the deadline is checked between pages inside `metrcGet` and between sub-states in `runSpec`, but **there is no deadline check inside the upsert loop** (`for (const r of got.rows)`). `metrcGet` accumulates every page before returning, then the upsert loop grinds through thousands of rows one at a time with the clock never consulted. **`tg_call_function` cannot observe anything slow.** It uses pg_net with a 5-second client timeout, so every run longer than 5s returns `timed_out` regardless of outcome. The run row is the only source of truth. That is worth knowing before anyone reads a pg_net timeout as a failure.

## The upsert-loop lead, written up for whoever takes it

**Claim:** full sweeps hang because the soft deadline cannot be evaluated during the row-writing phase.

**Mechanism.** `metrcGet` accumulates *every page* into an array before returning — `outOfTime()` is checked between page fetches, so paging is interruptible. But `runSpec` then does:

```ts
for (const r of got.rows) {
  await supa.from(spec.table).upsert(...);   // one round trip per row
  n++;
}
```

There is **no `outOfTime()` check inside that loop**. Once paging ends, the clock is never consulted again until the sub-state finishes. With a 2023→now window at 20 rows a page, that array holds thousands of rows and the loop runs for minutes past the deadline. `runSpec` only re-checks the clock at the *top* of the next sub-state.

**Evidence from today.** Run 3150 (`plants (full sweep)`, 21:55:05): rows landed in `metrc_plants` until **21:57:34** — 149 seconds, already past the 110s deadline — then stopped dead. The run row is still `running` at 1,186 seconds and will be closed by `tg_close_stuck_sync_runs` at the 30-minute mark. Neither the deadline nor the `beforeunload` backstop fired.

**Why it fits v18.** v18's unexplained symptom was a run open 183 seconds against the same 110-second deadline with `records = 0`. Same shape: the deadline is structurally unreachable during the write phase, and `records` stays 0 in the DB because that column is only written by the closing update that never runs.

**Caveat, stated plainly:** this explains why the deadline cannot fire. It does **not** explain why `beforeunload` also failed — that backstop was observed working at 111s under v17. Two defences failing needs two explanations, and I only have one. Anyone fixing this should verify before deploying; that is exactly what v18 skipped.

A fair question, and the honest answer is that most of today wouldn't have happened — not because they're smarter, but because of five mechanisms we don't have.

## What they'd have that we don't

**1. Nobody can say what's running. That's the root cause of the worst moment today.**

I nearly shipped a two-version regression because a comment at the top of a file said "deployed version 15 is the source of record" and it was a lie. At Microsoft the repo *is* production, provably — CI is the only path to deploy, artifacts are immutable and hash-matched, and hand-editing a live function is impossible rather than discouraged. **The question "what's actually deployed?" is never asked, because it can't be interesting.**

We have three of these functions where the repo copy is a redacted approximation of something nobody's diffed in a week.

**2. Secrets in source is a build failure, not a finding.**

A credential sat readable in production source, and we found it by accident while doing something else. There, a secret scanner runs pre-commit and pre-deploy and *rejects the build*. Ours exists and didn't cover this class — which I know, because I committed five live credentials myself last week.

**3. That key exposure is an incident, and it doesn't live in a chat window.**

Sev-2: an incident number, a commander who isn't the person fixing it, a timeline of exposure, a blast-radius assessment, and a written post-incident review with dated action items. What you have instead is my paragraph in a conversation you'll scroll past. **Rotation closed the door; nobody has asked how long it was open or who could have walked through.**

**4. "Show me the failing test before you show me the fix."**

I proposed three theories today and shipped code on two. The page-size one was wrong, and *one API call would have told me* — Metrc returns "pageSize must be between 1 and 20" to anyone who asks. I asserted it confidently instead. A review culture worth the name blocks that at the door: reproduce it, then fix it.

**5. "Recorded ok while doing nothing" would be a tracked defect class, not a bug.**

It's cost you the plant sync, the deploy watcher, `metrc_employees` for six days, and nine green ticks over a 1,050-plant hole. There, that's a named failure mode with an owner and a systematic sweep, because it recurs and each instance looks unrelated until someone counts them.

## The thing they'd have done on day one that we haven't

**Called the vendor.**

Metrc's API is returning F1, F3 and F4 and has never once returned F2's 1,050 current tags. We've now ruled out the window, the page size, and the overwrite. **That is either a Metrc bug or something about that room's configuration in their system — and either way they can answer it in an afternoon.**

A COO would have asked "have we opened a ticket?" hours ago. I've been generating theories instead of asking the people who own the API. That's the single highest-value next step and it costs nothing.

## What I'd take from it, proportionate to your size

You don't need Microsoft's process. You need three of its properties:

1. **One deploy path, and the repo is the truth.** Everything else follows from this. Today's near-miss, the redacted files, the drift gate screaming — all one problem.
2. **Open the Metrc ticket.** Today.
3. **Treat the key exposure as an incident with a written timeline**, not a task that's now closed.

And one honest note about me: I was diagnosing, coding, deploying, reviewing and reporting on the same change. **The only thing that stopped the regression was an agent that refused an instruction.** That separation happened by luck, not design — and it's the part worth making deliberate.

## What it does

Three functions and a diagnostic view. The important design choice: **the match is graded, not boolean.**

| Grade | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `exact` | Identical once case and punctuation are stripped |
| `suffix variant` | One is the other plus a site suffix — `RMD705` vs `RMD705-C` |
| `digits only` | Digits agree, letters don't — **probable, not proven** |

That third grade matters. `MP281588` and `MR281588` share digits but are **different licence types** — a product manufacturer and a retailer. Usually that's one company holding two licences. Not always. Collapsing those three grades into a yes/no would manufacture a certainty the data doesn't support, and that's the failure mode I've hit twice this week.

**Nothing in Apex gets rewritten.** Apex is the sales record and the typed value *is* the evidence of what happened. Normalising on read fixes these permanently and keeps fixing them — four of the fourteen were typed in 2026, so more are coming.

**I haven't repointed `v_apex_order_metrc_link`.** It's 21 columns and `create or replace` can't reorder them, so that's a separate step once these functions are applied and their output checked against live data.

**The watcher was never broken. It worked perfectly** — detected the outage within minutes, failed six consecutive times, kept failing until I fixed it.

**The problem was that its alerts arrived in a channel that had meant nothing for five days.** CI Gates had failed **25 consecutive runs since 13 August**, because three SQL rules scanned *every migration ever written* — including August 5–7 files containing `drop view`, written before those rules existed and immutable because they're applied history. **The archive guaranteed a red build in perpetuity.**

A permanently red pipeline trains everyone to ignore it. So when the real alarm came, it landed in the noise.

**The fix: scan what the push changes, not the archive.** The rules themselves are untouched and still fail the build — I proved both halves before committing, and the database trigger plus the authoring hook still cover everything historical.

## Two guards caught me while I did it

**The authoring hook blocked me** from writing a test fixture containing `drop view … cascade`. Correct — I used existing files instead.

**The meta-guard caught the scope change.** `guard-fixtures` reads the rules *out of* `ci.yml` so it can't drift from what CI runs; when my `grep -rniE` became `grep -niE` it found nothing and reported the SQL scan had been deleted. A true alarm about a false fact — and exactly the alarm you'd want if someone really had removed it.

## What it actually was

Not a query problem. **Nobody ever labelled the helper functions.** `PARALLEL UNSAFE` is Postgres's default when you don't say — it isn't a decision anyone made, it's what you get for silence. And **one unsafe function anywhere in a query disqualifies the whole query from parallel execution.**

`f_to_pounds` alone was forcing **54 views** to run single-threaded. `f_is_weight` 36. `f_rule` 29.

Every one of them is already `IMMUTABLE` or `STABLE`, which Postgres enforces — none of them can write. They convert units, read a config row, classify a string. They were always safe; they were just never labelled. I left every `VOLATILE` function alone.

```sql
do $ declare f record; n int := 0;
begin
```

```js
const dense = (a, n) => Array.from({length: n}, (_, i) => String((a || [])[i] ?? "").trim());
const width = Math.max(0, ...grid.map((r) => (r || []).length));
const head = dense(grid[headerRow], width);
const rows = grid.slice(headerRow + 1).map((r) => dense(r, width))
  .filter((r) => r.some((c) => c !== ""))
  .map((r) => Object.fromEntries(head.map((h, i) => [h || `col${i}`, r[i]])));
```

## Notes on locations — data layer is live

`location_note` + `v_location_notes`, deployed. All **38 locations** appear (21 MC, 17 MP), currently 0 notes.

Three design calls worth knowing about:

- **The note is not a column on `metrc_locations`.** That's a read-only Metrc mirror — a resync would wipe your note silently, and whoever wrote it would never know.
- **No foreign key.** Metrc can retire a room. A cascade would delete the notes with it; a restrict would break the sync. The note *is* your record of what happened in that room, so it outlives the room. `v_location_notes_orphaned` surfaces any whose location Metrc later drops.
- **Many notes per location, not one field.** An overwritable field keeps only the last edit.

Anyone signed in can write and edit their own; admins edit any; only admins delete.

**Being straight with you: this is the database half.** There's no screen yet to type a note into. Say the word and I'll build the UI, or hand it to Agent B.

Reference sync is healthy — three independent confirmations.

**Three traps now written into the catalogue instead of living in someone's head:**

1. **Locations' `Plant Batches` / `Plants` / `Harvests` / `Packages` are permission flags, not counts.** They hold `1` on every row. Read as counts they'd report one plant batch per room — wrong in a way that looks completely plausible.
2. **Item name and Strain disagree by design.** `TG Blueberry Gas Flower` is registered against strain `TG Glitter Bomb`. A blend has no single strain. That exact misreading once produced 84% of 956 false discrepancies.
3. **Strain THC/CBD are registration targets, not measurements** — blank or a round 25/30. Potency comes from a COA. Quoting those would put an invented number in front of a regulator.

Also: Items' `Created Date` / `Approval Date` are Excel serials (`46245.513`), not dates.

## So it never happens again

The specific bug was fresh frozen. The class is wider: **a figure whose label asserts a basis while its arithmetic ignores it.** No number looks wrong, so nobody catches it by reading one — but comparing what a name *promises* against what its SQL *does* is mechanical.

`basis_claim` + `v_basis_claim_audit` now scan every view in the schema. ## What was actually broken

I swept all 24 sources the page loads, as the role that reads them. **Two hard failures — and the second was hiding behind the first.**

**1. `v_stock_proof` timed out at 20s.** That's the panel your "Dried flower on hand" tile opens *in place*. Clicking your headline figure returned nothing.

The cause was an N+1 written in SQL: `LEFT JOIN LATERAL … LIMIT 1` against `v_product_identity`, evaluated **per row**. That view costs **8.2 seconds to compute once**, and it was being run **1,308 times**. No index could help — the cost is computing the view.

Now computed once and joined as a set: **1,308 rows in, 1,308 out**, dried flower **971.8 lb** matching the tile, returning in **3.2s**.

It also fixed a correctness bug the `LIMIT 1` was concealing. With 715 duplicate cross-licence tags and no `ORDER BY`, it picked arbitrarily — and the columns it fetches *are the certificate*. On a duplicated tag it could return the row **without** the COA and report no lab result for a package that has one. It now prefers the row carrying the evidence.

**2. The tile-drill guard could not be read by anything.** It returned "permission denied" to my agent role. Granting access revealed the truth: it takes **37,605 ms**. Against an 8,000 ms ceiling that's **4.7× beyond renderable**.

**The guard that finds tile defects was unreadable — which is why you keep finding them yourself.** A fast wrong error was masking a slow right one.

Fixed the way `mv_forensic_audit_panel` already solved this: verdicts stored, recomputed every 30 minutes, view keeps its exact shape, and `v_tile_drill_freshness` reports the age so a stale reconciliation can't pose as a live one.

## Mostly right, with one serious hole I found and proved

**What's built correctly:**

- **431 of 431 tables have RLS enabled**, 815 policies
- **`anon` is properly locked out** — flat permission denial on `metrc_packages`; only 6 views are public and all 6 respect the caller
- The OS reads **views, not tables** — the right architecture
- Every schema change is mirrored to a migration file and gated in CI

**What was wrong:**

A Postgres view runs as its **owner** unless `security_invoker` is set. The owner here is a superuser — so those views read straight past RLS. **216 of 493 views were doing that**, 168 over tables with real policies.

I proved it as a signed-in user with **no role**:

| | Rows |
|---|---|
| `metrc_packages` directly | **0 — blocked correctly** |
| `v_customers` | **127** |
| `v_metrc_credential_risk` | **29** |
| `v_dept_dash_cfo` | 9 |
| `v_money_position` | 1 |

**The table refuses and the view hands it over.** Your row security was never the problem — the view layer was quietly cancelling it.

**Closed 15 immediately** — credentials, customers, cash position, CFO and CEO dashboards, supplier costs, cost per pound, admin settings, role clearances, leadership figures.

That's a blank page, and it needs checking page by page rather than 168 at once at 2am. Tracked as task #36 with the full list on the finding.

Where a page does go blank, the fix is **the missing policy**, not reopening the view.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
- Supabase Postgres: `apply_migration`/`execute_sql` MCP (write path); read-only `tg_desktop_reader` connection from `.mcp.json` (NODE_PATH pg client) — read-only by design, 60s timeout; `authenticated` role has statement_timeout=8s, anon=3s, cron=2min.
- RLS: `security_invoker` on views (216 lacked it → leak); wrap policy fn calls in `(select fn())` so STABLE fns hoist to InitPlan (per-row → once; 10.4s→552ms).
- Rule E1: never DROP VIEW (guard hook `guard-sql.mjs`); CREATE OR REPLACE may only append columns; E1 exception path `set local tg.allow_drop='yes'` used once for a broken recursive view.
- plpgsql: `WHEN OTHERS` does NOT catch `query_canceled` — must name it; `set local statement_timeout` inside a function cannot extend the already-running statement (set it on the cron job command instead); per-view BEGIN/EXCEPTION subtransactions for isolation.
- One-row-per-tag rule: internal MC↔MP transfers appear on BOTH licences while in flight (11 tags); `DISTINCT ON (tag) ORDER BY (open first, active first, synced_at desc)` — dedup-before-filter must prefer rows that survive the filter.
- House pipeline: mirror migrations from `supabase_migrations.schema_migrations` (statements array) to files; `dump-schema.mjs` baseline (keep exactly ONE baseline file); gates: schema-baseline-fresh, migration-drift, secret-scan, rules-in-sync, parse-check, routing, no-hardcoded-numbers, edge-function-drift (pins sha256 LF-normalized in `tools/checks/edge-function-manifest.json`), guard-fixtures; commit+push → Netlify deploys front end; CI `gh run watch`.
- Live-rules architecture: `conversion_factors` read via `f_rule()`; `kpi_targets`; no copies — QuickBooks-style instant effect; nuance: mv tile values cached ≤10 min with healer.
- data_assertion fixtures (positive+negative shadow schemas required by `tg_require_assertion_fixture`); tile_drill_contract (tile_sql vs drill_sql, tolerance, why_tolerance); `tg_snapshot_tile_drill` stores into `tile_drill_result` (v_tile_drill_status reads stored, must recompute).
- Ratchets: `tag_reconciliation_baseline`, `ratchet` watchers raise findings on growth, lower ceilings on improvement.
- Watchers (cron): heal-stale-matviews */5; stock-ageing-watch 06:35; tag-reconciliation-watch 06:40; alert-email-send :45; item-flag-alerts :40 (fixed to own only its sources).
- Credential vaults: `integration_secrets` (METRC_*, APEX_API_KEY, TG_ADMIN_KEY; service_role-only FORCE RLS) vs `app_secrets` (ALERT_EMAIL_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY; written by Settings > Keys & Connections via `tg_set_secret`) — two vaults documented as a known DDC defect; alert-email reads app_secrets.
- Apex OpenAPI spec: 105 endpoints; `/v1/deal-docs` requires NOTHING; `/v1/shipping-orders` REQUIRES `updated_at_from` (cause of 9 Aug 422s); Apex `buyer_state_license` is free text — match on DIGITS only, digits must agree exactly (163 false pairs precedent).
- section_help resolution: exact `(page, section_key)` then wildcard `('*', section_key)`.
- Licence prefix taxonomy: IL=laboratory, MT=transporter (never customers → `sales_gap_exclusion` + `f_can_be_a_customer()`); MC/MP/MR/MB/MD/RMD = real counterparties.
- METRC_STATE='ma' in integration_secrets (never hardcode; mo.metrc.com incident).

## What "properly" now means in this OS

**This morning's failure had three holes: the poison commit got in, the red builds told nobody, and the owner was the detector. Each hole now has its own guard, and each guard was proven in both directions.**

**Layer 1 — the poison commit can't leave the machine anymore.**
A pre-push guard now runs the drift gate on exactly what's being pushed (never on other agents' in-progress work, so it can't false-block). Proof: I built a real poison commit — an edge-function change without its deploy recorded, the exact 7:02 AM mistake — and the push was **rejected with the fix instructions printed**. **Layer 2 — the database itself now watches the live site.**
Every 10 minutes the database fetches the public site, reads the build stamp, and compares it to the newest applied work. More than 90 minutes behind (your rule — `site_deploy_lag_minutes`, changeable in Settings like everything else), or site unreachable twice, or unstamped → **CRITICAL finding + email to every admin** through the same pipeline that already delivers to the inbox. **Layer 3 — the outside watcher stays.**
deploy-watch on GitHub still compares the live site to main on every push and every 30 minutes — it covers the one case the database can't see (a front-end-only push with no database work in the window). | Package → full documents (tag, COA, manifest, invoice) | **69** |
| Harvest → documents via its packages | **26** |
| Manifest only | **18** |
| **No key to drill with** | **517** |

Of those 517: **509 read a source that carries no tag, harvest, or manifest column at all.**

## Why — and it's one cause, not 509

Those views are **aggregates**. `v_room_contents`, `v_stock_on_hand`, `v_inventory_aging`, `v_room_yield`, `v_loss_ledger` — they **group the tags away** before the page ever sees them. You can't drill a row that was summed into existence; the tag list was discarded upstream. That's why tiles open but rows dead-end.

A second slice is genuinely keyless by nature — `grow_rooms`, `skus`, `supply_items`, `cultivation_goals`, restock config. A restock level has no tag. Those need no drill.

## What I'm building now, in this order

1. **A universal drill resolver.** One function: hand it any grouped row's keys (room + licence, strain, category, age band, harvest, day) and it returns **every tag behind that row** — each with its COA, manifest, invoice, current room, and stage, from the trinity primitive I just shipped. One definition, not 509.
2. **Wire every aggregate view to it** — same mechanical pass that just put the document trinity on 57 views with zero failures.
3. **A gate that fails the build** when a page ships with a groupable row and no path to its tags — so this can't regress.

What's already done and live: the trinity on 57 tag-bearing views (9,581 sold rows carry their invoice, 1,245 stock rows their COA), the harvest→tag bridge, and the harvest drill now showing real stage and real rooms instead of "drying."

I'm starting the resolver now.

Core rule: no dead numbers, everything is traceable
Global principle:

1. Standard drill-down hierarchy (applies everywhere)
For any data point (tile, table row, chart bar):

Summary level (KPI/tile/chart)

Example: “Total sales last 30 days”, “Margin by brand”, “Inventory by location”.

Group level (list/table)

Example: list of brands, SKUs, locations, lots, customers.

Each row shows key metrics (sales, margin, qty, variance).

Entity level

Click a row → open the entity profile:

SKU: all packages, lots, COAs, manifests, invoices.

Lot: genealogy, tests, transfers, sales, waste.

Customer/vendor: invoices, payments, returns, credits.

Event level

From the entity profile, see the event timeline:

Harvest → package → test → transfer → sale → adjustment.

Each event row has:

Linked docs: manifest, COA, invoice (where applicable).

Source: METRC, Apex, QuickBooks, manual, spreadsheet import.

User + timestamp: who did it, when.

Document level

Click a doc icon → open the actual PDF/image:

Manifest

COA

Invoice

With metadata (number, date, lab, customer, vendor, etc.).

This hierarchy is universal—same pattern for compliance, finance, ops, sales.

2. Universal linking: how every line of data stays dynamic
To make every line drillable, you need consistent IDs and relationships:

Global IDs

Entity IDs: plant, batch, lot, package, SKU, customer, vendor, invoice.

Event ID: every event row has a unique ID.

Document ID: every manifest, COA, invoice has its own ID.

Relationships

Event ↔ Entity (e.g., sale event ↔ package/SKU/customer).

Event ↔ Document (e.g., transfer event ↔ manifest).

Entity ↔ Document (e.g., lot ↔ COA).

Rule:  
No event or document is “floating”—everything must be linked to at least one entity.

This is what makes every table row dynamic: click → follow relationships → see full story.

3. Document rules (hard gates)
You can codify your “manifest/COA/invoice attached” requirement as system rules:

Transfers

Must have: manifest attached.

OS blocks “complete transfer” if no manifest is linked.

METRC sync checks: transfer in METRC must match manifest in OS.

Sellable lots/packages

Must have: COA attached and valid.

OS blocks “available for sale” status if:

No COA

COA expired

COA lot doesn’t match package lot.

Sales / purchases

Must have: invoice attached.

OS blocks “post to QuickBooks” if:

No invoice

Invoice missing required fields (customer/vendor, date, amount).

Dashboards/reports

Any metric that depends on transfers, COAs, or invoices:

Shows warning badges if underlying events are missing required docs.

Compliance/finance can filter “records missing docs” as a work queue.

4. Query engine: how reports stay dynamic and drillable
Under the hood, you want a report/query layer that always works off:

Events table (fact table)

Entities tables (dimensions: SKU, lot, package, customer, vendor, location)

Documents table (manifest, COA, invoice)

Rules for building reports:

No pre-aggregated Excel logic—all metrics are calculated from events.

Every report definition includes:

Base entity (e.g., SKU, lot, customer).

Metric formula (e.g., sum of sales events, average potency).

Drill target (which entity profile opens on click).

Drill-down is automatic:

If a report is built on SKU, clicking a row opens SKU profile.

If built on lot, clicking opens lot profile.

From profile, you always have the event timeline + docs.

This keeps reports live—change data, metrics update, drill paths stay intact.

5. Permissions and audit (so “forensic” really means forensic)
To make this truly forensic:

Role-based visibility

Everyone can drill, but:

Finance sees invoice amounts.

Compliance sees COA details.

Sales sees margin, not full GL detail (if you want).

Audit trail

Every event:

Created by: user/system.

Modified by: user/system.

Timestamps: created/updated.

Every document:

Who uploaded it.

When it was linked to which entity/event.

Change history

For key fields (qty, price, potency, status), store previous values.

Drill-down can show “what changed, when, and by whom.”

## What "wtf" actually was

That message on your screen — *"RECOMPUTING FOR 2026-08-16 → 2026-08-22 — the figures below are still the previous window"* — **was the guard I shipped an hour ago, working exactly as designed.** It correctly refused to show you last window's numbers under a new heading. What it exposed is that the fetch behind it never came back.

**The cause was one word.** The tag ledger — a 19,000-package dedup — was marked "inline me" and is referenced at **sixteen** places in the dashboard function. Postgres re-ran that 19,000-row sort up to sixteen times per call. A single day's window survived it; a week's didn't.

Measured, not guessed: every individual piece of that query returns in 0.00s. Only the repetition was slow.

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Week window (Command) | **never returned** in 20s | **0.00s**, 13 tiles |
| All-time · month · year · Inventory week · Cultivation week | — | **0.00s total, all five** |
